blocks.x: Cost per transaction, per customer, per inference — engineering metrics with P&L consequences.
FinOps is unit economics, not cost cutting. Allocation architecture precedes optimization; unattributed spend is unmanageable spend.
Commitment strategy is a utilization game: 90%+ coverage without idle waste.
Architectural cost reviews redesign expensive paths before deployment, not after invoices.
Where it breaks in practice: lift-and-shift economics: estates migrated without unit-cost telemetry, so the savings case quietly erodes while the bill grows more opaque.
The strongest counter-case, stated fairly: the unit-economics thesis can excuse under-provisioning that costs more in incidents than it saves in compute. FinOps is a balance, not a crusade.

In delivery, this thesis becomes a specific discipline: infrastructure is treated as a product: versioned, observable, costed, and handed to your team with runbooks rather than folklore. Every program in the Cloud, Edge & Platform domain carries the same obligations — a signed baseline, named gate criteria, and evidence generated by running the system rather than preparing for a meeting.
